newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan watchdog faces test on brokerage scandal.
newsitem.headline: Japan watchdog faces test on brokerage scandal.

text.p: Japan's securities watchdog, born of scandals which swept the nation's brokerages six years ago, faces a tough test as it tackles the latest threat to the industry's credibility, legal experts said on Friday.

The Securities and Exchange Surveillance Commission (SESC) is investigating top brokerage Nomura Securities Co Ltd over suspected illegal deals with a corporate client linked by Japanese media to a "sokaiya" racketeer.

But some lawyers question whether the body and other authorities are equal either to the current task or future challenges as Japan moves ahead with its sweeping "Big Bang" plan to deregulate financial markets by the year 2001.
"This is a real test of fire for the SESC," said an analyst at a foreign brokerage.

On Friday, only hours after Nomura president Hideo Sakamaki and two board members resigned over the scandal, a police official told a parliamentary panel that the National Police Agency was gathering information on the affair.

On Thursday Daiwa Securities, number two in the domestic industry, said the SESC was conducting what the brokerage termed a routine inspection, adding that this was not related to any suspicions over its trading practices.
Shozo Wakabayashi, secretary-general of the SESC's executive bureau, declined comment on Friday when asked in parliament about probes of brokerages other than Nomura.

But Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka said the watchdog would likely look into newspaper reports that the same racketeer-related firm said to be involved in the Nomura case held accounts at Daiwa, Nikko Securities Co Ltd and Yamaichi Securities Co Ltd. Daiwa declined to comment on the report and Nikko and Yamaichi officials were not immediately available.

Grilled by an opposition party member as to why securities scandals keep on happening, Wakabayashi insisted the SESC was doing its best. "The SESC was set up to secure fairness and transparency in securities deals and cultivate a healthy securities market. We have acted in that light and will continue to do so," he said.

But some analysts and lawyers said the need to conduct simultaneous probes could strain SESC resources, test the commitment of authorities and challenge the ability of Japan's legal system to cope with such cases.

"There are too few staff, too few cases brought, too few convictions and too little serious jail-time served," said an international lawyer in Tokyo. "My perception is that there has been no change since the SESC was set up."
"Ultimately, the sanction that gets serious attention is for an individual to go to jail. For a company to be fined or suspended from doing business doesn't do much," he added.
The SESC, set up in 1992 in response to heavy criticism of authorities for failing to prevent the huge brokerage scandals, is modelled on the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission.
But with 89 staff, the SESC has only a fraction of the investigative strength of its U.S. counterpart.

The Japanese watchdog lacks the right to take punitive action itself but can recommend that the finance minister mete out administrative punishment and can ask prosecutors to take legal action against possible criminal violations.

The SESC has filed complaints with prosecutors six times since its inception, according to its latest report issued last October. All cases went to court but of the five in which verdicts have been handed down, the heaviest penalties were fines and suspended jail sentences, the report said.
"There are lots of laws and authorities can use them if they try," said securities lawyer Seijiro Watanabe. "But the penalties are extremely light."

Lawyers and industry experts say preventing, exposing and punishing financial misdeeds will be even more critical as Japan opens its markets to more competition through its "Big Bang" programme, but some worry whether officials and political leaders fully recognise the need for change.
"It is more critical, but until someone upstairs realises that, I'm not sure things will change," the international lawyer said. "A light should be going on in someone's head."
